inputs.need:
I am a clinical biochemist and the laboratory's quality lead at a hospital with a busy emergency department. Our haemolysis index flags about 8 percent of emergency department potassium samples as haemolysed, against about 1.5 percent from the wards and outpatient phlebotomy. Haemolysed samples are rejected or reported with a comment, the test is repeated, and emergency physicians complain about the delays. Most emergency samples are drawn through a newly placed peripheral intravenous cannula, while ward samples are drawn by phlebotomists with a needle, and emergency samples travel by pneumatic tube while outpatient samples are carried by hand.

The emergency department wants to keep drawing from cannulas because it saves a second needle stick, especially for children and people with difficult veins. The published studies point in different directions: some report several-fold higher haemolysis with cannula draws, others find little difference when a particular technique or a small syringe is used. I am torn between doing a systematic review of haemolysis by collection method and site, so that any policy rests on the whole literature, and doing a retrospective study of our own laboratory information system data, where we can see collection site, collector role and tube transport for every sample since 2023. I need help choosing, and in either case with defining the outcome and handling the ways the studies differ.
inputs.constraints: No research funding; the laboratory quality lead and one biochemistry trainee can give about 80 hours between them before June 2027; any change to emergency department collection policy needs the joint approval of the emergency and laboratory directors.
localFacts: The laboratory information system records collection site, collector role, tube transport route and the haemolysis index for every sample since January 2023; it does not record whether a sample was drawn through a cannula or a needle.
In the last 12 months, 8.1 percent of emergency department potassium samples and 1.5 percent of ward and outpatient samples had a haemolysis index above the rejection threshold.
The hospital librarian runs database searches for the laboratory on request (standing agreement LIB-LAB-2025).
The emergency and laboratory directors must jointly approve any change to emergency collection policy.

response.title: Haemolysis by collection method and site: choosing between a systematic review and a local laboratory data study
response.subtitle: Design not yet settled: a systematic review of collection method or a retrospective laboratory data study
response.statement: Emergency department potassium samples haemolyse at about five times the ward rate (8.1 against 1.5 percent), causing rejected results, repeat draws and delays. Emergency samples differ from ward samples in collection method (cannula rather than needle), collector (nurses rather than phlebotomists) and transport (pneumatic tube rather than hand-carried). The emergency department wants to keep cannula draws to spare patients a second needle stick. The laboratory needs to decide whether a policy on collection method is justified, and by which kind of study.
response.whoAffected: Emergency patients, especially children and people with difficult veins; emergency nurses and physicians; laboratory staff who reject and repeat samples.
response.whatHurts: Rejected potassium results delay decisions and cause repeat needle sticks; a policy banning cannula draws would add needle sticks for the patients least able to tolerate them.
response.currentPractice: Cannula draws with standard vacuum tubes by emergency nurses; high-speed pneumatic tube transport; rejection or comment on haemolysed samples; no routine monitoring by collection site.
response.whyNow: Emergency physicians are pressing the laboratory about delays, and the directors must jointly decide any policy change.
response.constraints: No research funding; the laboratory quality lead and one biochemistry trainee can give about 80 hours between them before June 2027; any change to emergency department collection policy needs the joint approval of the emergency and laboratory directors.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Emergency patients get reliable potassium results from a single needle stick whenever possible.
response.summary: Problem framed; the design is left unresolved between a systematic review and a local retrospective study until the evidence is reviewed.

records.title: Haemolysis in blood drawn through peripheral intravenous catheters versus venepuncture in adult emergency patients
records.authors: Saarinen-Obi K, Delacroix-Mwangi R, Brandt-Oyelaran T
records.abstract: We compared 620 potassium samples from adult emergency patients, 310 drawn through a newly inserted peripheral intravenous catheter and 310 by venepuncture with a needle, over six months in one emergency department. Haemolysis, defined as a haemolysis index above the analyser's rejection threshold, occurred in 19.6 percent of catheter draws and 4.2 percent of venepuncture samples. Catheters of 20 gauge or smaller haemolysed more often than larger ones. Samples were drawn by emergency nurses using standard vacuum tubes. Allocation to method was by clinical situation, not by chance, and the authors could not account for difficult venous access.

records.title: Catheter-drawn samples collected with a low-vacuum tube or small syringe: haemolysis compared with venepuncture in a randomised crossover study
records.abstract: In 260 emergency patients who needed both a peripheral intravenous catheter and blood tests, we drew one sample through the new catheter using a low-vacuum tube or a small syringe and one by venepuncture, in random order. Haemolysis occurred in 3.9 percent of catheter samples and 3.1 percent of venepuncture samples, a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95 percent CI -1.4 to 3.0). Potassium results differed by less than 0.1 mmol per litre on average. All samples were drawn by two trained research nurses, which may not reflect routine emergency practice.

records.title: Pneumatic tube transport and haemolysis index: the effect of tube speed and distance
records.abstract: We measured the haemolysis index in 1,480 paired samples sent from the emergency department to the laboratory either by hand or by a pneumatic tube system at two speed settings. Haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 2.0 percent of hand-carried samples and 5.6 percent of samples sent at the high speed setting. Reducing the tube speed brought the rate down to 2.4 percent without a clinically important delay in delivery. Longer routes with more bends were associated with higher haemolysis. The study was done in one hospital with one tube system.

records.title: Blood sampling through peripheral intravenous catheters and haemolysis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
records.authors: Rasmussen-Adeyemi J, Lindqvist-Tanaka H, Oduya-Kowalski B, Ferreira-Mbeki S
records.abstract: We included 24 studies comparing haemolysis in samples drawn through peripheral intravenous catheters with venepuncture samples. The pooled odds ratio for haemolysis with catheter draws was 3.4 (95 percent CI 2.1 to 5.5), with very high heterogeneity (I-squared 88 percent). The effect was smaller in studies using low-vacuum tubes or syringes and in studies with trained collectors. Only four studies were randomised; most were before-after or cross-sectional comparisons at high risk of bias. Definitions of haemolysis ranged from visual inspection to analyser index thresholds, and the authors rated certainty as very low.

records.title: Haemolysis in paediatric emergency samples by collection method
records.abstract: We reviewed 410 paediatric emergency samples collected through a newly inserted intravenous catheter, by venepuncture or by capillary puncture. Haemolysis above the analyser threshold occurred in 11 percent of catheter samples, 7 percent of venepuncture samples and 16 percent of capillary samples. Catheter draws avoided a second puncture in most children. The abstract does not state when the samples were collected, how collection method was chosen or whether collectors differed between methods, and no full paper has been identified. Results are presented as percentages without confidence intervals.

records.title: Who draws the sample matters: haemolysis rates by collector role in the emergency department
records.abstract: Across 9,850 emergency department samples over 12 months, haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 2.1 percent of samples drawn by phlebotomists, 7.8 percent drawn by nurses and 9.6 percent drawn by physicians. Most nurse and physician samples were drawn through catheters, so collector role and method could not be separated. After a 30-minute training session for emergency nurses, their haemolysis rate fell to 4.4 percent over the next six months. The comparison was uncontrolled and the training coincided with a change of tube supplier.

records.title: Monitoring haemolysis by collection site with laboratory information system data: a retrospective analysis of 1.2 million samples
records.authors: Grieve-Nwosu R, Haddad-Lindgren T, Kaur-Whitfield A
records.abstract: We analysed 1.2 million samples from four hospitals using laboratory information system fields for collection site, collector role and transport route. Haemolysis above the rejection threshold occurred in 6.9 percent of emergency department samples and 1.8 percent of inpatient samples. Variation between collection sites was larger than variation between analysers. The data could not identify whether samples were drawn through a catheter, so the effect of collection method could not be estimated. The authors recommend site-level haemolysis rates as a routine quality indicator rather than as evidence about collection method.

records.title: Recommendations on preanalytical sample quality and haemolysis management from a laboratory medicine working group
records.abstract: A working group of 12 laboratory specialists and emergency clinicians reviewed evidence on haemolysis and agreed recommendations by consensus. The group recommends monitoring haemolysis rates by collection location, using analyser haemolysis indices rather than visual inspection, and training all collectors. It makes no recommendation for or against drawing samples through peripheral intravenous catheters because the evidence was judged conflicting. The group notes that reducing repeat venepuncture matters to patients with difficult venous access and to children, and asks laboratories to publish haemolysis rates by site so that practices can be compared.

response.synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level; one is an undated conference abstract whose method quality cannot be assessed. The evidence on catheter draws conflicts: a non-randomised emergency study found 19.6 against 4.2 percent haemolysis, a randomised crossover study with low-vacuum tubes or syringes found almost no difference, and a meta-analysis of 24 mostly non-randomised studies reported a pooled odds ratio of 3.4 with very high heterogeneity that shrank with better technique and trained collectors. Transport speed and collector role each change haemolysis and are entangled with collection method in routine data. Laboratory information system data show site differences but cannot identify catheter draws. A consensus group declined to recommend for or against catheter draws. The conflict is plausibly explained by technique, but the certainty of any single estimate is very low.
response.gradeRationale: Mostly non-randomised comparisons at high risk of bias, very high inconsistency across studies, and indirectness from trained research collectors; only one small randomised study. Certainty that catheter draws themselves raise haemolysis in routine practice is very low.
response.summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; the evidence conflicts; claim c3 records the conflict with high uncertainty; overall certainty very low.

response.reading: The emergency excess in haemolysis has three candidate causes that travel together: cannula draws, collector role and pneumatic tube transport. The published evidence on cannula draws conflicts (claim c3), plausibly because technique and collector training vary, while transport speed has its own effect (claim c4). The laboratory's own data can separate site, collector role and transport but not collection method (claim c5), so a local study cannot answer the method question on which a policy would rest.

response.finer: Feasible within 80 hours with librarian support if restricted to comparative studies; interesting to the emergency and laboratory directors; novel in its focus on technique subgroups; ethical as a literature review; relevant because it decides a joint policy.

response.rationale: The policy question is whether drawing through a catheter itself raises haemolysis, and under what technique. The published estimates conflict (c1, c2) and the conflict appears to depend on technique and collector (c3), which a systematic review with pre-specified subgroups can examine. A local retrospective study cannot answer the question because the laboratory system does not record collection method, as in the retrieved four-hospital analysis (c5), and transport confounds site comparisons (c4). The local data are better used afterwards for site-level monitoring of any change.
alternatives: Retrospective study of local laboratory data (refused for the method question: collection method is not recorded; kept for monitoring)
Local randomised comparison of draw techniques (refused: no research funding and the review may make it unnecessary)
Adopt the working group's recommendations without a review (refused: they make no recommendation on catheter draws)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: An individual participant data meta-analysis or a local trial would cost far more than the 80 hours available; a systematic review with subgroups is the simplest design that can explain the conflict.

decision.statement: Conduct a systematic review with meta-analysis of haemolysis in catheter-drawn versus venepuncture samples, with subgroups by tube type, catheter gauge, collector training and transport, and use local laboratory data only for site-level monitoring.
decision.question: Which study should inform the emergency collection policy?

response.overview: Systematic review with meta-analysis of comparative studies of haemolysis in blood drawn through peripheral intravenous catheters versus venepuncture, registered before screening, with pre-specified subgroups by technique, catheter gauge, collector training and transport.
response.population: Blood samples from adults and children in emergency or acute care settings in comparative studies of any design (randomised, crossover, cohort, before-after and cross-sectional).
response.exposure: Collection through a newly inserted or existing peripheral intravenous catheter, with tube type or syringe recorded.
response.procedures: Librarian-designed searches of three databases and conference proceedings from 2000 to 2026 under agreement LIB-LAB-2025. Two reviewers (the quality lead and the trainee) screen and extract independently, resolving disagreements by discussion. Risk of bias is assessed with RoB 2 for randomised comparisons and ROBINS-I for non-randomised ones; certainty is rated with GRADE for each outcome.

response.designSummary: Random-effects meta-analysis of log odds ratios for haemolysis, randomised and non-randomised studies analysed separately, with pre-specified subgroup analyses and meta-regression.
response.sampleSize: The prior review found 24 studies to 2022; with later studies about 30 to 35 are expected. Subgroup analysis and meta-regression are planned only for effect modifiers with at least ten studies, because with I-squared near 88 percent fewer studies give unstable estimates. A 95 percent prediction interval is reported alongside every pooled estimate so that the likely range in a new setting is visible.
response.primaryAnalysis: Random-effects model (restricted maximum likelihood with Hartung-Knapp adjustment) for the odds ratio of haemolysis with catheter draws versus venepuncture, separately for randomised and non-randomised comparisons.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Subgroups by tube type or syringe, catheter gauge, collector training and transport; meta-regression on the proportion of low-vacuum draws if at least ten studies report it; sensitivity analysis restricted to analyser index definitions; descriptive paediatric results.

response.multiplicity: One primary estimate per design group; subgroup findings are reported as hypothesis-generating with an interaction test.

response.title: Haemolysis in blood samples drawn through peripheral intravenous catheters versus venepuncture: a systematic review and meta-analysis with technique subgroups
response.abstract: Objective: to estimate the association between catheter draws and haemolysis and to examine whether technique, catheter gauge, collector training and transport explain conflicting results. Design: registered systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis. Results and conclusions will be written after the analysis.
response.introduction: Published estimates of haemolysis with catheter draws range from several-fold to almost no difference. Emergency departments value catheter draws because they avoid extra needle sticks, while laboratories see rejected samples.
response.methods: Librarian-designed search, dual screening and extraction, RoB 2 and ROBINS-I, GRADE certainty, random-effects meta-analysis separately for randomised and non-randomised studies, four pre-specified effect modifiers and prediction intervals.
response.results: Not yet written. The section will report study flow, study characteristics, pooled estimates with prediction intervals by design group, subgroup analyses and GRADE certainty.
response.discussion: The discussion will state whether technique explains the conflict and what that means for an emergency collection policy that weighs haemolysis against extra needle sticks.
response.limitations: Mostly non-randomised primary studies with heterogeneous definitions; limited paediatric data.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will be worded by GRADE certainty.
response.summary: PRISMA-structured draft with results left empty until analysis.
